title: The Infinite Curve
tagline: His spirals and concave facades bent the rules of space itself.

scenes.text: Rome, 1630s. Francesco Borromini works in the shadow of Bernini — despised by the establishment, yet obsessed with a different kind of beauty.

Where Bernini uses grand columns and classical order, Borromini bends walls into concave curves. His church of San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane fits inside one pillar of St. Peter's — but feels infinite.

challenge.fact: Borromini (1599–1667) invented a new architectural language: walls that curved inward and outward, spaces that expanded and contracted as you moved through them, and geometry derived from interlocking triangles rather than squares. His buildings feel alive — as if the stone itself is breathing.
challenge.instruction: Borromini's walls refuse to stand straight. Guess the five-letter word for what his façades do where Bernini's stand firm.

scenes.text: He uses geometry — triangles, ovals, hexagons — as the hidden skeleton of his buildings. Nothing is arbitrary. Every curve obeys a mathematical relationship.

challenge.instruction: Every Borromini plan closes on itself, built from triangles and ovals with nothing left to chance. Ride the knight across every square and end one leap from where you began, a figure as closed as his geometry.
challenge.fact: Borromini's geometry was rooted in medieval sacred mathematics — he derived church plans from the proportions of the equilateral triangle, believing divine truth was encoded in geometric relationships. His buildings are not just beautiful; they are arguments about the nature of space and the presence of God within it.

params.title: The Hidden Skeleton
params.intro: Borromini drew his plans from interlocking triangles and ovals, every curve closing on itself. Visit every square once — and finish a knight’s move from where you began (the ringed square).
params.fact: Borromini built the plan of San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane (begun 1634) from two equilateral triangles sharing a base, with an oval traced inside them.

scenes.text: His patrons appreciate him grudgingly. He works for the Oratorians, the Sapienza University — commissions he can keep, commissions Bernini disdained.

challenge.instruction: For the Oratorians Borromini is building the hall where Rome gathers to hear sacred stories sung. Put the sections of an oratorio of the day in the order the story unfolds.
challenge.fact: Borromini designed the Oratory of the Filippini beside the Chiesa Nuova from 1637 for the Congregation of the Oratory founded by St Philip Neri. Its concave brick façade hides the hall where the congregation's musical prayer meetings — the gatherings that gave the oratorio its name — were held.

scenes.text: He clashes bitterly with Bernini throughout his life. Their rivalry becomes legendary — the classical versus the radical, the celebrated versus the misunderstood.

challenge.instruction: Rome has become a board for two players: Bernini's fountain on one side of Piazza Navona, Borromini's Sant'Agnese on the other. Take the rivalry square by square and line up five before your rival does.
challenge.fact: On Piazza Navona Bernini's Fountain of the Four Rivers (1648–1651) stands before Borromini's Sant'Agnese in Agone (begun 1653). The tale that Bernini's River Plate raises a hand to shield himself from the falling church is a legend: the fountain was finished before Borromini began the façade. The rivalry itself was real — Borromini believed Bernini took credit for his ideas.

params.title: Piazza Navona
params.intro: A rivalry played out on one square: you are black and move first. Five or more in a row wins.
params.fact: Bernini’s Fountain of the Four Rivers (1651) and Borromini’s Sant’Agnese in Agone face each other across Piazza Navona, the ancient stadium of Domitian.

scenes.text: Borromini died by suicide in 1667. But his spiraling lantern on Sant'Ivo della Sapienza, his concave-convex facades, his impossible interiors — they outlived every critic.

challenge.instruction: Borromini is dead, but his churches still curve across the city. Walk his Rome and cross every bridge exactly once.
challenge.fact: Borromini's last great work, Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza (1642–1660), rests on a star-hexagon plan of two interlocking triangles and is crowned by a spiralling lantern. He died in August 1667 after falling on his sword; his buildings outlived every critic.

scenes.speaker: Francesco Borromini
scenes.text: Two face-down cards: one at St Petersburg, one at London. We cannot see who they are until we attack, and an attack reveals every card at the location. The Tech Race already runs at St Petersburg; you hold a card to start one at London.

challenge.instruction: Fight lesson 5 · Face Down. Win two attacks: fight at St Petersburg where the Tech Race is running, then carry the fight to London by starting your own event there.
challenge.fact: A card on the board can be public (face up) or private (face down). A private card hides its identity and stats from rivals until an attack reveals every card at that location. Your own cards deploy face down; Go Public when being seen helps you.
